name: Photon Energy (E=hf)
description: Gives the energy of a single photon from its frequency using the Planck relation, energy equals Planck's constant times frequency. Higher-frequency light carries proportionally more energy per photon.
notes: Frequency must be in hertz; the resulting energy in joules is extremely small for a single photon. Divide by the electron charge to convert to electron-volts if desired.

name: Photon Energy (E=hc/λ)
description: Computes a photon's energy from its wavelength, using Planck's constant times the speed of light divided by the wavelength. Shorter wavelengths carry more energy, so the energy is inversely proportional to wavelength.
notes: Wavelength must be in meters (e.g. 5e-7 m for green light). Use the speed of light in the medium if not in vacuum; the result is in joules.

name: de Broglie Wavelength
description: Gives the de Broglie wavelength of a particle from its mass and velocity, expressing the wave nature of matter as Planck's constant divided by momentum. Faster or heavier particles have shorter wavelengths.
notes: This non-relativistic form uses momentum m times v; at speeds near light, relativistic momentum is needed. The wavelength is measurable only for very light particles like electrons.

name: Photoelectric Effect (Max Kinetic Energy)
description: Computes the maximum kinetic energy of an ejected photoelectron from Einstein's photoelectric equation, KEmax = h·f − φ, where h·f is the photon energy and φ is the material's work function. The result is the leftover energy after freeing the electron.
notes: If h·f is below the work function φ the result is negative, meaning no electrons are emitted. All energies here are in joules and f is in hertz.

name: Stopping Potential
description: Computes the stopping potential in the photoelectric effect, V = (h·f − φ)/qe, the voltage that just halts the most energetic photoelectrons. It equals the maximum electron kinetic energy divided by the elementary charge.
notes: Meaningful only when h·f exceeds the work function φ; otherwise no emission occurs. Energies are in joules and qe in coulombs, giving volts.

name: Threshold Frequency
description: Computes the threshold frequency for the photoelectric effect, f0 = φ/h, the minimum light frequency that can eject electrons from a material with work function φ. Below this frequency no photoemission occurs.
notes: φ is in joules and h in J·s, giving f0 in hertz. Frequencies at or above f0 are required regardless of light intensity.

name: Work Function from Threshold
description: Computes a material's work function from its threshold frequency, φ = h·f0, the minimum energy needed to free an electron from the surface. It is the photon energy exactly at the emission threshold.
notes: f0 is in hertz and h in J·s, so φ comes out in joules; divide by 1.602e−19 to express it in electron-volts.

name: Max Photoelectron Speed
description: Computes the maximum speed of an ejected photoelectron by equating its kinetic energy to h·f − φ, giving v = √(2·(h·f − φ)/m). It converts the leftover photon energy into electron speed.
notes: Requires h·f greater than φ, or the radicand is negative and no electrons escape. This is a non-relativistic estimate; m is the electron mass in kg.

name: Planck Energy Quantum
description: Computes the energy of a single quantum (photon) of radiation from its frequency using the Planck relation, E = h·f. It gives the smallest packet of energy carried by light of that frequency.
notes: f is in hertz and h in J·s, giving energy in joules. Energy scales linearly with frequency, so higher-frequency light carries more energy per photon.

name: Photon Energy from Wavelength
description: Computes photon energy from its wavelength using E = h·c/λ, combining the Planck relation with c = f·λ. Shorter wavelengths correspond to higher-energy photons.
notes: λ is in meters and the result is in joules; use the vacuum speed of light for c. Energy is inversely proportional to wavelength.

name: Bohr Energy Level
description: Computes the energy of an electron in level n of a hydrogen-like atom in the Bohr model, E = −13.6·z²/n² electron-volts, where z is the atomic number. The negative sign indicates the electron is bound to the nucleus.
notes: Applies to single-electron (hydrogen-like) atoms only; n is a positive integer. The result is in eV, and energy approaches zero as n grows large.

name: Bohr Orbit Radius
description: Computes the radius of the electron's orbit in level n of a hydrogen-like atom in the Bohr model, r = a0·n²/z, where a0 is the Bohr radius and z the atomic number. The orbit grows with the square of the level number.
notes: Valid for single-electron atoms; n is a positive integer and a0 ≈ 5.29e−11 m. Higher nuclear charge z pulls the orbit inward.

name: Bohr Orbital Velocity
description: Computes the electron's orbital speed in level n of a hydrogen-like atom in the Bohr model, v = 2.188e6·z/n m/s, where the constant is the ground-state speed of hydrogen. The electron moves slower in higher levels.
notes: Applies to single-electron atoms; n is a positive integer. The constant 2,188,000 m/s is roughly the fine-structure constant times the speed of light.

name: Hydrogen Transition Energy
description: Computes the energy released or absorbed when an electron moves between two levels in a hydrogen-like atom, ΔE = 13.6·z²·(1/n1² − 1/n2²) electron-volts. A positive value corresponds to emission from the upper to the lower level.
notes: n1 is the lower level and n2 the upper; the result is in eV. This assumes single-electron (hydrogen-like) atoms in the Bohr model.

name: Rydberg Wavelength
description: Computes the wavelength of light emitted or absorbed in a hydrogen transition using the Rydberg formula, λ = 1/(R·(1/n1² − 1/n2²)), where R is the Rydberg constant. It links the two energy levels to a spectral line.
notes: n1 is the lower level and n2 the upper (n2 > n1) so the denominator is positive. R is in 1/m, giving λ in meters.

name: Mass-Energy Equivalence (E=mc^2)
description: Computes the rest energy equivalent of a mass using Einstein's relation E = m·c², the total energy contained in a mass at rest. Even a tiny mass corresponds to an enormous energy because c is squared.
notes: m is in kg and c is the speed of light in m/s, giving energy in joules. This is rest energy; kinetic energy from motion is additional.

name: Rest Energy in eV
description: Computes the rest energy of a particle, E = m·c², and expresses it in electron-volts by dividing the joule value by the elementary charge. For an electron this gives about 511000 eV (0.511 MeV).
notes: Mass must be in kilograms and c in metres per second so the energy is in joules before the division. Dividing by qe (in coulombs) converts joules to eV, not to keV or MeV.

name: Mass Defect Binding Energy
description: Applies E = Δm·c² to convert a nuclear mass defect into its equivalent binding energy in joules. The mass defect is the difference between the summed masses of the free nucleons and the actual nuclear mass.
notes: The mass defect must be entered in kilograms; if given in atomic mass units it has to be converted first. The result is the total binding energy of the whole nucleus, not per nucleon.

name: Binding Energy from Mass Defect (MeV)
description: Converts a mass defect expressed in atomic mass units directly into binding energy in MeV, using the conversion factor that one unified mass unit equals about 931.5 MeV/c². It is a shortcut for E = Δm·c².
notes: The mass defect must be in atomic mass units (u), not kilograms. The factor 931.5 already includes c², so no further multiplication by the speed of light is needed.

name: Binding Energy per Nucleon
description: Divides the total nuclear binding energy by the mass number to give the average binding energy holding each nucleon in the nucleus. This value peaks near iron and indicates nuclear stability.
notes: The mass number A is the total count of protons and neutrons and is dimensionless. Keep the total binding energy in MeV so the result comes out in MeV per nucleon.

name: Nuclear Radius
description: Estimates the radius of an atomic nucleus using R = r0·A^(1/3), where the cube root of the mass number reflects that nuclear volume is roughly proportional to the number of nucleons. The result is a length in metres.
notes: The mass number A is dimensionless; the radius constant r0 (about 1.2 femtometres) sets the scale. This is an empirical approximation assuming a nearly constant nuclear density.

name: Radioactive Decay Law
description: Gives the number of undecayed nuclei remaining after time t through exponential decay, N = N0·exp(−λt), where λ is the decay constant. The population falls to 1/e of its start after a time 1/λ.
notes: The decay constant λ and the time t must use consistent time units so that λt is dimensionless. This assumes a single decay mode with a constant probability per nucleus.

name: Radioactive Activity
description: Calculates the activity of a radioactive sample, A = λ·N, the number of decays per second produced by N nuclei each with decay constant λ. The result is in becquerels (decays per second).
notes: The decay constant must be in inverse seconds so the activity comes out in becquerels. Activity is proportional to the number of nuclei present, so it decreases as the sample decays.

name: Half-life to Decay Constant
description: Converts a half-life into the corresponding decay constant using λ = ln(2)/t½. The decay constant is the probability per unit time that a given nucleus decays.
notes: The result carries the inverse of whatever time unit the half-life uses, so a half-life in seconds gives a decay constant in inverse seconds. ln(2) is about 0.693.

name: Decay Constant to Half-life
description: Converts a decay constant into the half-life through t½ = ln(2)/λ, the time over which half of a large sample of nuclei decays. It is the inverse of the half-life-to-decay-constant relation.
notes: The half-life comes out in the time unit matching the decay constant, so a λ in inverse seconds yields a half-life in seconds. Half-life is independent of the amount of material present.

name: Compton Shift
description: Gives the increase in photon wavelength after Compton scattering off a stationary electron, Δλ = h/(m·c)·(1 − cos θ), where θ is the scattering angle. The shift is largest for back-scattering (θ = π).
notes: The scattering angle must be in radians. The shift depends only on the angle, not on the incident wavelength, and is zero for forward scattering (θ = 0).

name: Compton Wavelength
description: Computes the Compton wavelength of a particle, λ = h/(m·c), a fundamental length scale set by its mass. For the electron it is about 2.43 picometres.
notes: Mass must be in kilograms and c in metres per second to give a length in metres. This is the maximum possible Compton shift divided by two, and it shrinks for heavier particles.

name: de Broglie Momentum
description: Finds the momentum associated with a matter wave of a given wavelength, p = h/λ, from de Broglie's relation. Shorter wavelengths correspond to larger momenta.
notes: The wavelength must be in metres so the momentum comes out in kilogram-metres per second. This links a wave property to a particle property and applies to any matter wave or photon.

name: de Broglie Wavelength (Accelerated Electron)
description: Gives the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated from rest through a voltage U, λ = h/√(2·m·qe·U). The denominator is the non-relativistic momentum gained from the electric field.
notes: The accelerating voltage is in volts and the result is in metres. This is a non-relativistic approximation and becomes inaccurate at very high voltages where the electron speed approaches c.

name: Heisenberg Uncertainty (Momentum)
description: Estimates the minimum uncertainty in momentum consistent with a given position uncertainty, using the Heisenberg limit Δp = ħ/(2·Δx). Smaller position uncertainty forces larger momentum uncertainty.
notes: This gives the lower bound of the product Δx·Δp = ħ/2, not an exact value, so real momentum spreads can be larger. Position uncertainty in metres yields momentum in kilogram-metres per second.

name: Relativistic Total Energy
description: Computes the total relativistic energy of a moving particle, E = m·c²/√(1 − v²/c²), which includes both its rest energy and kinetic energy. The energy diverges as the speed approaches c.
notes: The velocity must be less than the speed of light or the square root becomes undefined. Here m is the rest mass, and subtracting m·c² would give the relativistic kinetic energy.

name: Relativistic Mass
description: Gives the velocity-dependent relativistic mass, m = m0/√(1 − v²/c²), which grows without bound as the speed approaches the speed of light. At low speeds it reduces to the rest mass m0.
notes: The speed must be below c so the denominator stays real and positive. Relativistic mass is an older convention; many modern treatments keep mass invariant and put the gamma factor with energy and momentum.

name: Energy-Momentum Relation
description: Applies the relativistic energy-momentum relation E = √((p·c)² + (m·c²)²) to find a particle's total energy from its momentum and rest mass. For a massless particle it reduces to E = p·c.
notes: Momentum in kilogram-metres per second and mass in kilograms give energy in joules. This holds for any speed and does not require knowing the velocity directly.

name: Time Dilation
description: Gives the dilated time interval measured in a frame where a clock moves, t = t0/√(1 − v²/c²), from the proper time t0 measured in the clock's own frame. Moving clocks are observed to run slow.
notes: The velocity must be less than c. The proper time t0 is the interval between two events measured at the same place in the clock's rest frame; the result is always longer than t0.

name: Proper Time
description: Recovers the proper time t0 = t·√(1 − v²/c²) from an observed time interval t in a frame where the clock moves at speed v. It is the time elapsed on the moving clock itself.
notes: The speed must be below c. Proper time is always shorter than the observed interval, and this is the inverse of the time-dilation relation.

name: Relativistic Velocity Addition
description: Combines two collinear velocities relativistically, (u1 + u2)/(1 + u1·u2/c²), so the result never exceeds the speed of light. At low speeds it reduces to the ordinary sum u1 + u2.
notes: Both velocities must be along the same line and below c; opposite directions need one entered as negative. Adding any speed to c still gives exactly c.

name: Gravitational Time Dilation
description: Gives the time interval measured by a clock at radius r near a mass, t = t0·√(1 − 2·G·M/(r·c²)), relative to a far-away clock reading t0. Clocks deeper in a gravitational well run slower.
notes: This Schwarzschild result assumes a non-rotating spherical mass and a clock at rest outside it. The term 2GM/(rc²) must be less than one, i.e. r must exceed the Schwarzschild radius.

name: Planck Length
description: Evaluates the Planck length √(ħ·G/c³), the fundamental length scale formed from the quantum constant ħ, the gravitational constant G, and the speed of light. It is about 1.6×10⁻³⁵ metres.
notes: Using the standard constant values reproduces the fixed Planck length; the variables are exposed only to show its construction. Below this scale, quantum-gravity effects are expected to dominate.

name: Relativistic Time Dilation
description: Computes the dilated time observed for a moving clock as the proper time divided by sqrt(1-(v/c)^2). A clock moving at speed v ticks slower, so more coordinate time elapses.
notes: Velocity must be less than the speed of light or the square root becomes undefined. Use consistent speed units; the effect is negligible until v approaches c.

name: Length Contraction
description: Gives the contracted length of a moving object as the proper length times sqrt(1-(v/c)^2). An object moving at speed v appears shortened along its direction of motion.
notes: Contraction occurs only along the direction of motion, not perpendicular to it. Velocity must be below c and use the same units as the speed of light.

name: Relativistic Momentum
description: Computes the relativistic momentum of a moving mass as m·v divided by sqrt(1-(v/c)^2). Momentum exceeds the classical value m·v and grows without bound as speed approaches c.
notes: Use SI units (kg, m/s) for momentum in kg·m/s. Velocity must be less than c. At low speeds the formula reduces to the classical p = m·v.

name: Lorentz Factor
description: Calculates the Lorentz factor gamma = 1/sqrt(1-(v/c)^2), the dimensionless factor governing relativistic time dilation, length contraction, and momentum. It equals 1 at rest and grows as speed approaches c.
notes: Velocity must be strictly less than the speed of light and in the same units. Gamma is always at least 1; it diverges as v tends to c.

name: Total Relativistic Energy
description: Gives the total energy of a moving mass as m·c^2 divided by sqrt(1-(v/c)^2), the rest energy multiplied by the Lorentz factor. It includes both rest energy and relativistic kinetic energy.
notes: Use SI units (kg, m/s) for energy in joules, with velocity below the speed of light. At v = 0 it reduces to the rest energy m·c^2.

name: Relativistic Kinetic Energy
description: Computes the kinetic energy of a moving mass using special relativity as m·c²·(gamma − 1), where gamma = 1/sqrt(1 − (v/c)²). Unlike the classical ½mv², it stays valid at speeds approaching the speed of light and gives the energy in joules.
notes: Velocity must be below the speed of light; at v ≥ c the square root becomes imaginary or undefined. At low speeds the result reduces to the classical ½mv².

name: Photon Energy
description: Computes the energy carried by a single photon of a given wavelength as Planck's constant times the speed of light divided by the wavelength. Shorter wavelengths carry more energy per photon, so ultraviolet photons are more energetic than infrared ones.
notes: Wavelength must be in meters; visible light is around 4–7×10⁻⁷ m. Equivalent to E = h·f using frequency f = c/wavelength; the result is per single photon in joules.

name: Particle in a Box Energy Level
description: Gives the quantized energy of a particle confined in a one-dimensional box, n²h²/(8mL²), from the quantum number, particle mass, and box width. Energy rises with the square of the quantum number.
notes: The quantum number n is a positive integer (1, 2, 3, …). Narrower boxes and lighter particles raise the levels sharply, and Planck's constant is built into the formula.

name: Quantum Harmonic Oscillator Energy
description: Gives the energy of a quantum harmonic oscillator, (n + 1/2)ħω, from the quantum number and angular frequency. Levels are equally spaced by ħω above a nonzero ground state.
notes: The quantum number n is a non-negative integer (0, 1, 2, …), and ω is angular frequency in rad/s. Even at n = 0 the energy is nonzero, the zero-point energy ħω/2.

name: Zero-Point Energy (Harmonic Oscillator)
description: Gives the zero-point (ground-state) energy of a quantum harmonic oscillator, ħω/2, from its angular frequency. It is the minimum energy the oscillator retains even at absolute zero.
notes: This is the n = 0 case of the oscillator energy, and it is never zero. The angular frequency ω must be in rad/s, not ordinary frequency in hertz.

name: Fermi Energy (Free Electron Gas)
description: Computes the Fermi energy of a free electron gas, (ħ²/2m)(3π²n)^(2/3), from the electron mass and number density. It is the energy of the highest occupied state at absolute zero.
notes: Uses the free-electron model, ignoring the periodic lattice potential. The density n is electrons per cubic meter, and the result depends on n to the two-thirds power.

name: Fermi Velocity
description: Computes the Fermi velocity, the speed of electrons at the Fermi surface, ħ(3π²n)^(1/3)/m, from the electron number density and mass. It sets the characteristic electron speed in a metal.
notes: Based on the free-electron model with density n in electrons per cubic meter. This is the speed at the Fermi level at absolute zero, not an average thermal speed.

name: Fermi Temperature
description: Computes the Fermi temperature, the Fermi energy divided by the Boltzmann constant, (ħ²/2mkB)(3π²n)^(2/3). It marks the temperature scale above which thermal effects rival quantum degeneracy.
notes: Based on the free-electron model; the Boltzmann constant is built into the formula. Density n is in electrons per cubic meter, and typical metals have Fermi temperatures of tens of thousands of kelvin.

name: Thermal de Broglie Wavelength
description: Computes the thermal de Broglie wavelength, h/√(2πmkBT), from particle mass and temperature. It is the length scale below which quantum effects dominate a gas of particles.
notes: Temperature must be in kelvin; the wavelength shrinks as mass or temperature rises. Quantum statistics matter when this wavelength approaches the interparticle spacing.

name: Quantum Concentration
description: Computes the quantum concentration, (mkBT/(2πħ²))^(3/2), from particle mass and temperature. It is the particle density at which quantum effects become significant in a gas.
notes: Temperature is in kelvin; the result is a number density (particles per cubic meter). A gas behaves classically only when its actual concentration is well below this value.

name: Reduced Compton Wavelength
description: Computes the reduced Compton wavelength of a particle, ħ/(mc), from its mass. It is a fundamental quantum length scale set by the particle's rest mass.
notes: This is the reduced form (using ħ), smaller than the ordinary Compton wavelength by a factor of 2π. The speed of light is built in, so only the mass is needed.

name: Compton Scattered Photon Energy
description: Gives the energy of a photon after Compton scattering off a stationary electron, from the incident energy, electron mass, and scattering angle. Larger angles transfer more energy to the electron and lower the photon energy.
notes: The scattering angle must be in radians, and mc² is the electron rest energy. At zero angle the photon keeps its full energy; at 180 degrees (π) it loses the most.

name: Heisenberg Uncertainty (Energy-Time)
description: Gives the minimum energy uncertainty from the energy-time uncertainty principle, ħ/(2Δt), for a given time uncertainty. A shorter time window implies a larger unavoidable spread in energy.
notes: This is the lower bound set by ΔE·Δt ≥ ħ/2; real spreads can be larger. The time uncertainty is in seconds, and the result is the minimum energy uncertainty in joules.

name: Heisenberg Uncertainty (Minimum Position)
description: Gives the minimum position uncertainty from the position-momentum uncertainty principle, ħ/(2Δp), for a given momentum uncertainty. A better-known momentum forces a larger spread in position.
notes: This is the lower bound set by Δx·Δp ≥ ħ/2; actual uncertainty can only be larger. Momentum uncertainty is in kg·m/s, and the result is the minimum position spread in meters.

name: Quantum Tunneling Probability (WKB)
description: Estimates the probability that a particle of mass m and energy En penetrates a rectangular potential barrier of height V and width L, using the WKB approximation. The result is the exponential transmission factor exp(-2·L·sqrt(2m(V-En))/hbar), a dimensionless number between 0 and 1.
notes: Valid only when En is below V (a classically forbidden barrier); energies must be in joules and L in metres. It is an approximation for a thick, smooth barrier and ignores the pre-exponential prefactor.

name: de Broglie Frequency
description: Gives the intrinsic de Broglie frequency associated with a particle of rest mass m, defined by equating its rest energy m·c² to h·f. The result f = m·c²/h is expressed in hertz.
notes: Uses the rest mass only, so it gives the frequency in the particle's rest frame; enter m in kilograms. This total (Compton) frequency is enormous even for an electron and is not the same as a matter-wave beat frequency.

name: Matter Wave Phase Velocity
description: Computes the phase velocity of the matter wave for a non-relativistic particle moving at velocity v, given by c²/v. Because v is less than c, the phase velocity exceeds the speed of light.
notes: The superluminal phase velocity carries no information or energy; signals travel at the group velocity. Enter v in metres per second and keep v below c for this simple form.

name: Bohr Magneton
description: Calculates the Bohr magneton, the natural unit of electronic magnetic moment, as e·hbar/(2m) for a particle of mass m. The result, in joules per tesla, sets the scale of an electron's magnetic response to a field.
notes: Uses the electron charge and mass; enter m in kilograms. Substituting the proton mass instead yields the much smaller nuclear magneton, not the Bohr magneton.

name: Electron Spin Magnetic Moment
description: Gives the magnitude of the spin magnetic moment for a spin quantum number s, as g·μB·sqrt(s(s+1)), where μB is the Bohr magneton. The result is in joules per tesla and grows with both the g-factor and the spin.
notes: Returns the total moment magnitude sqrt(s(s+1)), not its projection g·μB·ms onto an axis. The g-factor is near 2.0023 for a free electron; enter s and g as dimensionless numbers.

name: Lande g-factor
description: Computes the Lande g-factor for an atomic state with quantum numbers J, S and L, using 1 + [J(J+1)+S(S+1)-L(L+1)]/[2J(J+1)]. This dimensionless factor scales the state's magnetic moment and its Zeeman splitting.
notes: Assumes LS (Russell-Saunders) coupling and breaks down for heavy atoms with strong spin-orbit coupling. J must be nonzero, and J, S, L are the state's total, spin and orbital quantum numbers.

name: Zeeman Energy Splitting
description: Gives the energy shift of a magnetic sublevel in an external field, g·μB·B·mj, where μB is the Bohr magneton and mj the magnetic quantum number. The result in joules is the linear Zeeman shift of that sublevel.
notes: This is the linear (weak-field) Zeeman term; strong fields require the Paschen-Back treatment. Enter B in tesla and use the appropriate Lande g-factor for the state.

name: Electron Larmor Frequency
description: Computes the angular Larmor precession frequency of an electron's magnetic moment in a magnetic field B, given by g·e·B/(2m). The result in radians per second is the rate at which the spin precesses about the field.
notes: The output is an angular frequency (rad/s); divide by 2π for hertz. Enter B in tesla and the electron mass in kilograms; g is the electron g-factor near 2.

name: Rotational Energy Level (Rigid Rotor)
description: Gives the rotational energy of a rigid rotor in quantum state J with moment of inertia I, as hbar²·J(J+1)/(2I). The result in joules gives the discrete rotational energy levels of a molecule.
notes: J is the rotational quantum number (0,1,2,...) and levels have spacing that grows with J. The rigid-rotor model ignores centrifugal stretching and vibration-rotation coupling; enter I in kg·m².

name: Molecular Vibrational Energy Level
description: Computes the energy of vibrational level v of a harmonic oscillator with wavenumber nu, as (v+1/2)·h·c·nu. The result in joules includes the zero-point energy at v=0.
notes: Wavenumber nu must be in 1/m (multiply cm^-1 values by 100). The harmonic model gives evenly spaced levels; real molecules show anharmonic narrowing at high v.

name: Hydrogen-like Energy Level
description: Gives the bound-state energy of a hydrogen-like atom with nuclear charge Z in principal level n, as -13.6057·Z²/n² electronvolts. The negative sign indicates a bound state below the ionization threshold.
notes: Applies to one-electron (hydrogen-like) ions only; it ignores fine structure and electron-electron repulsion. Z is the atomic number and n=1,2,3,...; the result is in eV.

name: Hydrogen Ionization Energy (Level n)
description: Gives the energy needed to ionize a hydrogen-like atom from principal level n, as +13.6057·Z²/n² electronvolts. It equals the magnitude of the binding energy of that level.
notes: For hydrogen (Z=1) at n=1 this gives 13.6 eV; higher n gives smaller ionization energies. Valid only for one-electron systems; enter Z and n as integers.

name: Rydberg Constant
description: Computes the Rydberg constant from fundamental constants and the electron mass m, as m·e⁴/(8·ε0²·h³·c). The result in 1/m sets the scale of hydrogen spectral line wavenumbers.
notes: This uses an infinitely heavy nucleus (R∞); using the reduced mass gives the slightly smaller R_H. Enter m in kilograms; the result is a wavenumber in 1/m.

name: Rydberg Formula (Energy Difference)
description: Gives the photon energy emitted or absorbed in a hydrogen-like transition between levels n1 and n2, as 13.6057·Z²·(1/n1²-1/n2²) electronvolts. A positive result corresponds to emission from the upper to the lower level.
notes: Here n1 is the lower level and n2 the upper; keep n2 greater than n1 for a positive emission energy. Applies to one-electron ions and ignores fine structure.

name: Moseley's Law (X-ray Frequency)
description: Estimates the frequency of a Kα characteristic X-ray from an element of atomic number Z, using Moseley's law with the 3/4 factor and screening constant b. The result in hertz scales as (Z-b)².
notes: The 3/4 factor and b≈1 are specific to the Kα line (n=2 to n=1). It is an empirical approximation; the screening constant differs for other X-ray series.

name: Duane-Hunt Law (Minimum X-ray Wavelength)
description: Gives the shortest wavelength of bremsstrahlung X-rays produced in a tube at accelerating voltage V, as h·c/(e·V). The result in metres corresponds to an electron converting all its kinetic energy into one photon.
notes: Depends only on the tube voltage, not the target material. Enter V in volts; the cutoff wavelength decreases as voltage increases.

name: Photoelectric Threshold Wavelength
description: Computes the longest light wavelength that can eject an electron from a surface with work function W, as h·c/W. Light longer than this wavelength cannot produce photoemission.
notes: Enter the work function W in joules (multiply eV values by 1.602e-19). The result is the threshold wavelength; shorter wavelengths give the ejected electrons extra kinetic energy.

name: Photoelectric Stopping Voltage
description: Gives the stopping voltage needed to halt photoelectrons emitted by light of frequency f from a surface of work function W, as (h·f-W)/e. The result in volts equals the maximum electron kinetic energy divided by the elementary charge.
notes: Enter W in joules and f in hertz. If h·f is below W the result is negative, meaning no electrons are emitted at that frequency.

name: Wien's Displacement Law (Frequency)
description: Gives the frequency at which a blackbody's spectral radiance peaks in the frequency domain, as 2.821439·k·T/h. The result in hertz rises linearly with the absolute temperature T.
notes: The 2.821 constant is the frequency-domain peak, which differs from the wavelength-domain peak (they are not related by c/λ=f). Enter T in kelvin.

name: Planck Oscillator Mean Energy
description: Computes the mean thermal energy of a Planck oscillator of frequency f at temperature T, as h·f/(exp(h·f/kT)-1). This is the Bose-Einstein average energy per mode, excluding zero-point energy.
notes: In the classical limit h·f << kT this approaches kT (equipartition). Enter f in hertz and T in kelvin; the result excludes the h·f/2 zero-point term.

name: Bose-Einstein Occupation Number
description: Gives the average number of bosons occupying a state of energy En at temperature T and chemical potential mu, as 1/(exp((En-mu)/kT)-1). It describes the equilibrium statistics of particles like photons and phonons.
notes: Requires En greater than mu, or the occupation diverges or turns negative. Enter energies in joules and T in kelvin; unlike fermions the value can exceed 1.

name: Fermi-Dirac Occupation Number
description: Gives the average occupation of a state of energy En at temperature T with Fermi level mu, as 1/(exp((En-mu)/kT)+1). The result lies between 0 and 1 and describes fermions such as electrons.
notes: At En equal to mu the occupation is exactly 1/2. Enter energies in joules and T in kelvin; the Pauli principle limits the value to at most 1.

name: Classical Electron Radius
description: Computes the classical electron radius, e²/(4π·ε0·m·c²), the size at which an electron's electrostatic self-energy would equal its rest energy m·c². The result is in metres.
notes: It is a classical order-of-magnitude scale, not the true physical size of the electron. Enter m in kilograms; using the electron mass gives about 2.82e-15 m.

name: Thomson Scattering Cross Section
description: Gives the total Thomson scattering cross section of a free electron, (8π/3)·re², where re is the classical electron radius. The result in square metres is the effective area for elastic photon scattering.
notes: Valid only in the low-energy limit where photon energy is much less than m·c²; higher energies require the Klein-Nishina formula. Enter re in metres.

name: Rutherford Scattering Cross Section
description: Computes the differential cross section for Coulomb scattering of a charge Z1 off a nucleus Z2 at kinetic energy En and angle theta, following Rutherford's formula. The result in m²/sr scales as 1/sin⁴(theta/2).
notes: The angle theta is in radians and must not be zero, where the cross section diverges. It is non-relativistic and treats the target nucleus as a fixed point charge; enter En in joules.

name: Electron Degeneracy Pressure (Non-relativistic)
description: Estimates the non-relativistic degeneracy pressure of an electron gas of number density n, as (hbar²/5m)·(3π²)^(2/3)·n^(5/3). This quantum pressure arises from the Pauli exclusion principle and supports white dwarfs.
notes: Valid only in the non-relativistic regime; at very high densities electrons become relativistic and pressure scales as n^(4/3). Enter n in 1/m³ and m in kilograms.

name: Debye Frequency
description: Gives the Debye cutoff angular frequency of lattice vibrations in a solid, vs·(6π²·n)^(1/3), where vs is the sound speed and n the atomic number density. The result in rad/s is the maximum phonon frequency in the Debye model.
notes: The output is an angular frequency (rad/s); divide by 2π for hertz. The Debye model assumes a linear dispersion and a single average sound speed; enter n in 1/m³.

name: Debye Temperature
description: Computes the Debye temperature of a solid, hbar·vs·(6π²·n)^(1/3)/k, which converts the Debye cutoff frequency into a temperature scale. Above it all lattice modes are thermally excited and heat capacity approaches the Dulong-Petit value.
notes: Uses a single average sound speed vs (m/s) and atomic number density n (1/m³). It is a model estimate; measured Debye temperatures vary with the averaging over acoustic branches.

name: Compton Edge Energy
description: Gives the maximum energy transferred to an electron in Compton scattering (the Compton edge) for an incident photon of energy En, when the photon back-scatters at 180 degrees. The result is in joules.
notes: This corresponds to 180-degree back-scattering, the maximum recoil energy; it is always less than the full photon energy En. Enter En and use the electron mass in kilograms.

name: Photon Number in a Pulse
description: Computes how many photons of frequency f are contained in a light pulse of total energy Ep, as Ep/(h·f). It simply divides the pulse energy by the single-photon energy.
notes: Assumes all photons share the same frequency f; a broadband pulse would need an average over its spectrum. Enter Ep in joules and f in hertz.

name: Blackbody Radiation Energy Density
description: Gives the total energy density of blackbody radiation at temperature T, (4σ/c)·T⁴, where σ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant. The result in J/m³ is the radiation energy stored per unit volume.
notes: This is the volumetric energy density, not the radiated power flux σ·T⁴ (W/m²); the two differ by a factor 4/c. Enter T in kelvin and note the strong T⁴ dependence.

name: Reduced Mass (Two-Body)
description: Computes the reduced mass of a two-body system, m1·m2/(m1+m2), which lets the relative motion of two interacting masses be treated as a single effective particle. The result is in kilograms.
notes: The reduced mass is always smaller than either individual mass. When one mass greatly exceeds the other it approaches the lighter mass; enter both masses in kilograms.

name: Proton Compton Wavelength
description: Gives the Compton wavelength of a particle of mass m, h/(m·c), here applied to the proton. It sets the length scale below which quantum-relativistic effects dominate for that particle.
notes: This is the standard (not reduced) Compton wavelength; the reduced form divides by 2π. Because the proton is heavy, its Compton wavelength is far smaller than the electron's; enter m in kilograms.

name: Hydrogen-like Orbital Radius
description: Computes the Bohr orbital radius of a hydrogen-like atom in level n with nuclear charge Z, as a0·n²/Z, where a0 is the Bohr radius. The result in metres grows as n² and shrinks with increasing Z.
notes: Based on the semiclassical Bohr model; in full quantum mechanics this is the most probable radius, not a sharp orbit. Enter Z and n as integers; a0 is 5.29e-11 m.

name: Sommerfeld Fine-Structure Splitting
description: Estimates the fine-structure energy correction for a hydrogen-like level with quantum numbers n and j, using Sommerfeld's formula with the fine-structure constant. The result in electronvolts is a small relativistic shift scaling as Z⁴.
notes: It is a first-order relativistic correction and is tiny compared with the gross level energy. j is the total angular momentum quantum number; the 137.036 factor is 1/α.

name: Rabi Frequency
description: Gives the Rabi angular frequency d·Ef/hbar, the rate at which a two-level system cycles between its states when driven by an electric field of amplitude Ef and coupled through dipole moment d. The result is in rad/s.
notes: This is the on-resonance Rabi frequency; detuning increases the effective (generalized) Rabi frequency. Enter the dipole moment d in C·m and field Ef in V/m; output is angular (rad/s).

name: Bohr Model Orbital Period
description: Gives the orbital period of an electron in the Bohr model for level n and nuclear charge Z, scaling as n³/Z². The result in seconds is the time for one classical revolution of the electron.
notes: Based on the semiclassical Bohr picture; the leading constant is the n=1 hydrogen period. Enter Z and n as integers; period grows steeply with n and shrinks with Z².

name: Orbital Angular Momentum Quantization
description: Gives the magnitude of the quantized orbital angular momentum, L = hbar*sqrt(l(l+1)), where l is the orbital angular momentum quantum number. The reduced Planck constant hbar is embedded as a literal (1.054571817e-34 J s).
notes: l must be a non-negative integer (0, 1, 2, ...) as required by quantum mechanics. The result is in joule-seconds, the SI unit of angular momentum.

name: Bohr Angular Momentum Quantization (mvr = nħ)
description: Computes the quantized value of orbital angular momentum for an electron in the n-th stationary state of the Bohr model of the atom. Bohr's postulate restricts the allowed angular momentum to integer multiples of the reduced Planck constant ħ.
notes: Applies to the (semi-classical) Bohr model, most accurately for hydrogen-like one-electron atoms/ions; n must be a positive integer (n = 1, 2, 3, ...).

name: Radioactive Mean Lifetime
description: Converts a radioactive half-life into the mean lifetime, th/ln(2). The mean lifetime is the average survival time of a nucleus and is always longer than the half-life. The result is in seconds.
notes: The mean lifetime is about 1.4427 times the half-life. Enter the half-life in seconds; the mean lifetime is the reciprocal of the decay constant.

name: Mean Lifetime from Decay Constant
description: Gives the mean lifetime of a decaying species as the reciprocal of its decay constant, 1/lam. It is the average time before a nucleus decays. The result is in seconds.
notes: The decay constant lam must be in 1/s. After one mean lifetime the surviving fraction has fallen to 1/e (about 37 percent).

name: Activity after Time
description: Computes the radioactive activity remaining after time t, A0·exp(-lam·t), where A0 is the initial activity and lam the decay constant. The result in becquerels follows exponential decay.
notes: The decay constant lam is in 1/s and t in seconds. Activity and number of nuclei decay with the same exponential; A0 sets only the initial scale.

name: Remaining Nuclei (Decay Constant)
description: Gives the number of undecayed nuclei remaining after time t, N0·exp(-lam·t), starting from N0 nuclei with decay constant lam. The result follows the exponential radioactive decay law.
notes: Enter lam in 1/s and t in seconds. The result is a count of nuclei; N0 must be the initial number at t=0.

name: Fraction Remaining (Number of Half-Lives)
description: Gives the fraction of a radioactive sample still remaining after time t, as 0.5^(t/th), where th is the half-life. Each half-life halves the remaining amount. The result is a dimensionless fraction between 0 and 1.
notes: t and th must share the same time unit, since only their ratio matters. The result gives the remaining fraction; multiply by 100 for a percentage.

name: Number of Half-Lives Elapsed
description: Computes how many half-lives have elapsed in time t, as the ratio t/th. This dimensionless count indicates how many times the sample has halved.
notes: t and th must use the same time unit; the result is generally not an integer. Raise 0.5 to this power to get the remaining fraction.

name: Q-value of Nuclear Reaction
description: Converts a nuclear mass difference dm (in atomic mass units) into the reaction Q-value, using dm·931.494 MeV/u. A positive Q means energy is released; a negative Q means the reaction is endothermic.
notes: The mass difference dm must be in unified atomic mass units (u); 931.494 MeV is the energy equivalent of 1 u. Use reactant minus product masses so that mass loss gives a positive Q.

name: Alpha Decay Q-value
description: Computes the energy released in alpha decay from the parent, daughter and alpha masses, as (Mp-Md-Ma)·931.494 MeV. A positive Q-value means the decay is energetically allowed.
notes: All masses must be in atomic mass units (u). Using atomic (rather than nuclear) masses is consistent because electron masses cancel in alpha decay.

name: Alpha Particle Kinetic Energy (Recoil)
description: Gives the kinetic energy carried by the emitted alpha particle in alpha decay, Q·(A-4)/A, after accounting for the recoil of the daughter nucleus of mass number A. The result is in MeV.
notes: A is the parent mass number, and the remaining fraction 4/A of Q goes to the recoiling daughter. This uses non-relativistic momentum conservation; enter Q in MeV.

name: Semi-Empirical Mass Formula (Binding Energy)
description: Estimates a nucleus's binding energy from the semi-empirical (liquid-drop) mass formula, combining volume, surface, Coulomb and asymmetry terms for mass number A and atomic number Z. The result is in MeV.
notes: This form omits the pairing term, so odd-even effects are not captured; coefficients vary between references. A and Z are integers and the result is the total binding energy.

name: SEMF Binding Energy per Nucleon
description: Gives the binding energy per nucleon from the semi-empirical mass formula, dividing the total liquid-drop binding energy by the mass number A. The result in MeV peaks near iron for stable nuclei.
notes: Omits the pairing term like the base formula; coefficients are model-dependent. Binding energy per nucleon indicates nuclear stability, highest around A=56.

name: Coulomb Energy Term (SEMF)
description: Computes the Coulomb repulsion term of the semi-empirical mass formula, 0.711·Z(Z-1)/A^(1/3), which reduces a nucleus's binding energy due to electrostatic repulsion among its Z protons. The result is in MeV.
notes: The Z(Z-1) form counts distinct proton pairs; some references use Z² instead. This term subtracts from binding energy and grows rapidly for heavy, high-Z nuclei.

name: Asymmetry Energy Term (SEMF)
description: Gives the asymmetry (symmetry) term of the semi-empirical mass formula, 23.7·(A-2Z)²/A, which penalizes nuclei with unequal numbers of protons and neutrons. The result in MeV reduces the binding energy.
notes: The factor (A-2Z) equals the neutron excess N-Z and vanishes for N=Z nuclei. This term subtracts from binding energy; the coefficient is model-dependent.

name: Surface Energy Term (SEMF)
description: Computes the surface-energy correction in the semi-empirical mass formula, which lowers a nucleus binding energy because nucleons at the surface have fewer neighbors. It scales as the nuclear surface area, proportional to A to the two-thirds power.
notes: The 17.8 MeV coefficient is an empirical fit and varies by parameterization. A is a dimensionless mass number; the term is a reduction of binding energy, so it appears with a minus sign in the full SEMF.

name: Geiger-Nuttall Law (log Decay Constant)
description: Estimates the base-10 logarithm of the alpha-decay constant using the Geiger-Nuttall relation, which links decay rate to the daughter atomic number Z and the alpha particle energy. Higher alpha energy gives a larger log decay constant and thus faster decay.
notes: Constants a and b are empirical and depend on the decay series; En is the alpha kinetic energy in MeV. The result is a base-10 logarithm of the decay constant, not the decay constant itself.

name: Nuclear Volume
description: Estimates the volume of a nucleus assuming it is a sphere whose radius follows R = r0 * A^(1/3) with r0 = 1.2 fm. The volume grows linearly with mass number A, reflecting the near-constant density of nuclear matter.
notes: A is the dimensionless mass number and the result is in cubic meters. The constant 1.2e-15 m (1.2 fm) is the standard nuclear radius parameter; other references use slightly different r0 values.

name: Nuclear Matter Density
description: Computes the mass density of nuclear matter by dividing the nuclear mass (mass number A times the atomic mass unit) by the volume of a sphere of radius r0 * A^(1/3). Because both mass and volume scale with A, the density is essentially independent of A.
notes: A cancels out, so the result is nearly constant at roughly 2.3e17 kg/m^3 for any nucleus. It uses r0 = 1.2 fm and treats nucleon mass as one atomic mass unit, ignoring binding-energy mass differences.

name: Coulomb Barrier (Fusion)
description: Calculates the Coulomb barrier height two nuclei must overcome to fuse, as the electrostatic potential energy of charges Z1 and Z2 at contact separation r0*(A1^(1/3)+A2^(1/3)). Higher charges or smaller nuclei raise the barrier.
notes: The result is in joules; divide by 1.602e-13 to convert to MeV. It uses point-charge Coulomb energy at the touching radius and neglects quantum tunneling that lets fusion occur below this energy.

name: Gamma-Ray Attenuation (Beer-Lambert)
description: Gives the transmitted gamma-ray intensity after passing through a material of thickness x, following exponential attenuation from the incident intensity I0. The linear attenuation coefficient mu sets how rapidly intensity drops with depth.
notes: mu and x must use consistent length units (here 1/cm and cm). This narrow-beam Beer-Lambert law ignores buildup from scattered photons, so it underestimates dose behind thick shields.

name: Half-Value Layer
description: Computes the half-value layer, the material thickness that reduces gamma-ray intensity to half, from the linear attenuation coefficient mu. It equals ln(2) divided by mu.
notes: Result units match the inverse of mu (here cm). Valid for monoenergetic narrow-beam geometry; for polyenergetic beams the effective HVL changes with depth due to beam hardening.

name: Tenth-Value Layer
description: Computes the tenth-value layer, the material thickness that reduces gamma-ray intensity to one tenth, from the linear attenuation coefficient mu. It equals ln(10) divided by mu.
notes: Result units are the inverse of mu (here cm). One TVL corresponds to about 3.32 half-value layers. Applies to monoenergetic narrow-beam attenuation without scatter buildup.

name: Photon Mean Free Path
description: Gives the photon mean free path, the average distance a photon travels before interacting, as the reciprocal of the linear attenuation coefficient mu. Larger mu means more frequent interactions and a shorter path.
notes: Result units are the inverse of mu (here cm). It represents an average; individual photon path lengths are exponentially distributed around this value.

name: Specific Activity
description: Computes the specific activity, the radioactive decay rate per gram of a pure isotope, from its half-life and molar mass. It combines the decay constant ln(2)/half-life with the number of atoms per gram from Avogadro number over molar mass.
notes: Half-life must be in seconds and molar mass in g/mol to give Bq/g. Assumes a pure single isotope; natural samples with mixed isotopes have lower specific activity.

name: Radiometric Age (Decay)
description: Determines the elapsed time since a sample formed from the ratio of initial to remaining amount of a radioactive nuclide, using its half-life. It inverts exponential decay: age equals half-life over ln(2) times ln(N0/N).
notes: N0 and N need only the same units since their ratio is used; half-life sets the output time unit (here years). Assumes a closed system with no gain or loss of parent or daughter besides decay.

name: Radiocarbon Age
description: Calculates a radiocarbon age from the ratio of initial to measured carbon-14 activity, using the 5730-year half-life of C-14. Age equals 5730 over ln(2) times ln(A0/Am).
notes: A0 and Am need only consistent activity units since the ratio is taken. This is the Libby-style decay age; calendar dates require calibration for past atmospheric C-14 variation.

name: Reaction Threshold Energy
description: Computes the minimum projectile kinetic energy needed for an endothermic nuclear reaction, from the reaction Q-value and the projectile-to-target mass ratio. The threshold exceeds the reaction energy deficit by the factor (1 + m/M) to conserve momentum.
notes: Meaningful only for endothermic reactions with negative Q; the absolute value of Q is used. This is the non-relativistic threshold in the lab frame, valid when kinetic energies are small compared to rest masses.

name: Nuclear Reaction Rate Density
description: Gives the number of nuclear reactions per unit volume per unit time as the product of target number density, reaction cross section, and incident particle flux. More targets, larger cross section, or higher flux all raise the reaction rate.
notes: Uses consistent SI units (targets per m^3, cross section in m^2, flux per m^2 per s) to yield reactions per m^3 per s. Assumes a thin target so the flux is not appreciably attenuated across it.

name: Macroscopic Cross Section
description: Computes the macroscopic cross section, the probability of interaction per unit path length, as the product of the number density of nuclei and the microscopic cross section. It represents the total interaction target area per unit volume.
notes: With number density in 1/m^3 and microscopic cross section in m^2 the result is in 1/m. It is additive over reaction types and isotopes when the corresponding cross sections are summed.

name: Neutron Mean Free Path
description: Gives the neutron mean free path, the average distance a neutron travels between interactions, as the reciprocal of the macroscopic cross section (number density times microscopic cross section). Denser material or larger cross section shortens the path.
notes: With number density in 1/m^3 and cross section in m^2 the result is in meters. It is an average for a single interaction type; combine cross sections for total interaction path length.

name: Neutron Flux Attenuation
description: Gives the neutron flux remaining after traveling a distance x through a medium, following exponential attenuation from the incident flux phi0. The macroscopic cross section Sig sets the rate at which flux is removed with depth.
notes: Sig and x must use consistent length units (here 1/m and m). This uncollided-flux form counts only neutrons that pass without interacting and ignores scattered neutrons returning to the beam.

name: Four-Factor Formula
description: Computes the infinite multiplication factor of a reactor as the product of the reproduction factor, thermal utilization, resonance escape probability, and fast fission factor. It gives the neutron multiplication per generation ignoring leakage.
notes: All four factors are dimensionless. This assumes an infinite medium with no neutron leakage; the effective multiplication factor also requires the fast and thermal non-leakage probabilities.

name: Six-Factor Formula
description: Computes the effective multiplication factor of a finite reactor as the infinite multiplication factor times the fast and thermal non-leakage probabilities. It measures whether the neutron population grows, holds steady, or shrinks per generation.
notes: All factors are dimensionless; a result of 1 means criticality. The infinite factor kinf here already bundles the four-factor formula, and the two non-leakage terms account for the finite reactor size.

name: Reactor Reactivity
description: Computes reactor reactivity, the fractional deviation of the multiplication factor from criticality, as (k - 1) divided by k. Positive values mean a supercritical, growing neutron population and negative values mean subcritical.
notes: The result is dimensionless and often expressed in dollars or pcm by scaling. Near criticality k is close to 1, so reactivity is approximately k - 1; small errors in k strongly affect it.

name: Absorbed Dose
description: Computes the absorbed radiation dose as the energy deposited by ionizing radiation divided by the mass of the absorbing material. One gray equals one joule per kilogram.
notes: Energy in joules and mass in kilograms give the dose in gray. Absorbed dose measures deposited energy only; biological effect additionally depends on radiation type and tissue, captured by equivalent and effective dose.

name: Equivalent Dose
description: Computes the equivalent dose by multiplying the absorbed dose by a radiation weighting factor that reflects the biological damage of the radiation type. It converts deposited energy in gray to a health-relevant dose in sievert.
notes: The weighting factor is dimensionless (about 1 for photons and electrons, up to 20 for alpha particles and neutrons). Numerically gray and sievert are equal, but they denote physically different quantities.

name: Effective Dose
description: Computes the tissue-weighted effective dose by multiplying the equivalent dose to an organ by its tissue weighting factor, which reflects that organ sensitivity to radiation-induced harm. The result expresses whole-body risk in sievert.
notes: The tissue weighting factor is dimensionless and the ICRP factors sum to 1 over all tissues. Total effective dose is the sum of this product over every irradiated organ, not a single organ alone.

name: Point Source Dose Rate (Inverse Square)
description: Estimates the dose rate from a point radioactive source as the dose rate constant times the source activity divided by the square of the distance. It follows the inverse-square law, so doubling distance quarters the dose rate.
notes: Units must match the dose rate constant (here GBq for activity, m for distance, giving mSv/h). Valid for an unshielded point source in air; it ignores attenuation and scatter buildup in intervening material.

name: Nuclear Magneton
description: Computes the nuclear magneton, the natural unit of nuclear magnetic moment, as the elementary charge times the reduced Planck constant divided by twice the proton mass. It sets the scale for magnetic moments of nucleons and nuclei.
notes: Uses the proton mass, unlike the Bohr magneton which uses the electron mass, making it about 1836 times smaller (roughly 5.05e-27 J/T). Mass in kilograms yields the result in joules per tesla.

name: Nuclear Magnetic Moment
description: Computes a nuclear magnetic moment as the nuclear g-factor times the nuclear magneton times the nuclear spin quantum number. It gives the magnetic moment along the spin axis in joules per tesla.
notes: The g-factor and spin I are dimensionless; 5.05e-27 J/T is the nuclear magneton. This uses the simple product form; the observable moment convention (maximum projection versus total) can differ by factors.

name: NMR Larmor Frequency
description: Computes the Larmor precession frequency of a nuclear spin in a magnetic field, as the gyromagnetic ratio times the field strength divided by two pi. This is the resonance frequency probed in nuclear magnetic resonance.
notes: Dividing by 2 pi converts the angular gyromagnetic ratio (rad per s per T) to an ordinary frequency in hertz. Use the angular gyromagnetic ratio here; some tables list gamma already divided by 2 pi.

name: Bateman Equation (Daughter Activity)
expression: N10 * lam1 * lam2 / (lam2 - lam1) * (exp(-lam1 * t) - exp(-lam2 * t))
description: Gives the daughter nuclide activity at time t in a two-step parent-daughter decay chain, using the Bateman solution. It combines exponential decay of the parent and daughter with initial parent nuclei N10 and the two decay constants.
notes: Requires distinct decay constants (lam2 not equal to lam1) or the formula diverges. Assumes no daughter present initially and a single parent-to-daughter branch; decay constants in 1/s and time in s.

name: Secular Equilibrium Daughter Activity
description: Gives the buildup of daughter activity toward secular equilibrium with a long-lived parent, as the parent activity times (1 - exp(-lamd*t)). The daughter activity rises and asymptotically approaches the constant parent activity.
notes: Valid only when the parent half-life greatly exceeds the daughter half-life, so the parent activity Ap is treated as constant. Decay constant in 1/s and time in s; at large t the daughter activity approaches Ap.

name: Fission Energy from Fuel Mass (U-235)
description: Estimates the total energy released if a given mass of uranium-235 fully fissions, by counting the atoms (mass over 235 times Avogadro number) and assigning about 200 MeV per fission. The result is the aggregate fission energy in MeV.
notes: Fuel mass in grams and 235 as the molar mass of U-235; 200 MeV per fission is a nominal average. It assumes complete fission of every atom, an idealization real reactors never reach.

name: Gamow Energy
description: Computes the Gamow energy, a characteristic energy scale governing Coulomb-barrier tunneling in charged-particle fusion, from the nuclear charges and the reduced mass of the pair. Larger charges or reduced mass raise this energy.
notes: Reduced mass in kilograms gives the result in joules; 137.036 is the inverse fine-structure constant and c is the speed of light. The Gamow energy sets the exponent in the barrier penetration factor.

name: Gamow Factor (Barrier Penetration)
description: Computes the Gamow factor, the exponential suppression of quantum tunneling through the Coulomb barrier, as exp of minus the square root of the Gamow energy over the relative energy. Higher relative energy gives a larger, less suppressed factor.
notes: EG and En must share the same energy unit since only their ratio matters. The result is a dimensionless probability-like factor between 0 and 1; it captures only the tunneling exponent, not the full reaction cross section.

name: Sommerfeld Parameter
description: Computes the Sommerfeld parameter, the dimensionless ratio of Coulomb interaction strength to kinetic scale for two charged nuclei, from their charges and relative velocity. It measures how strongly the Coulomb barrier suppresses low-energy fusion.
notes: The result is dimensionless; velocity in m/s. Larger values mean stronger Coulomb suppression and exponentially smaller tunneling, so slow, highly charged nuclei are hardest to fuse.

name: Neutron Diffusion Length
description: Computes the neutron diffusion length, the characteristic distance a thermal neutron diffuses before being absorbed, as the square root of the diffusion coefficient over the absorption cross section. Larger absorption shortens this length.
notes: Units must be consistent (here D in cm and Sa in 1/cm give cm). It is a diffusion-theory quantity for thermal neutrons; the mean square distance to absorption is six times the square of this length.

name: Reactor Period (Prompt)
description: Estimates the prompt reactor period, the time for neutron population to change by a factor of e, as the prompt neutron lifetime divided by (k - 1). A multiplication factor just above 1 gives a very short, rapidly growing period.
notes: Lifetime in seconds gives the period in seconds; the result is negative for subcritical k below 1. This prompt-only estimate ignores delayed neutrons, which in practice greatly lengthen the actual reactor period.

name: Nuclear Mass Defect
description: Computes the nuclear mass defect, delta_m = Z*mp + (A-Z)*mn - M, the difference between the summed mass of separate protons and neutrons and the actual measured mass of the nuclide. This missing mass corresponds to the nuclear binding energy via E=mc^2.
notes: All masses should be entered in atomic mass units (u). A larger mass defect means a more tightly bound, more stable nucleus.

name: Effective Half-Life
description: Computes the effective half-life of a radiotracer in the body, Teff = (Tphys*Tbio)/(Tphys+Tbio), combining radioactive decay with biological clearance. It is used in nuclear medicine to predict how quickly administered activity falls in a patient.
notes: Tphys and Tbio must use the same time unit, and the result shares that unit. The effective half-life is always shorter than either the physical or biological half-life alone.

name: Rapidity from Velocity
description: Computes the relativistic rapidity from the velocity ratio beta = v/c, as half the natural log of (1+beta) over (1-beta). Rapidity is the additive measure of velocity in special relativity that grows without bound as beta approaches 1.
notes: Beta is dimensionless and must satisfy -1 < beta < 1, or the logarithm is undefined. Unlike velocities, rapidities add linearly under collinear Lorentz boosts, which is their main advantage.

name: Relativistic Aberration of Light
description: Computes the observed direction of a light ray in a frame moving at beta relative to the source, giving the aberrated angle from the emission angle theta. Relativistic motion shifts light forward, concentrating it toward the direction of travel.
notes: Angles are in radians and beta is dimensionless with magnitude below 1. This is the relativistic aberration formula; at beta near 1 most light appears strongly beamed into a narrow forward cone.

name: Transverse Doppler Effect
description: Computes the observed frequency of a source moving transversely to the line of sight, as the source frequency times sqrt(1 - beta^2). It is a purely relativistic redshift caused by time dilation, with no classical counterpart.
notes: Beta is dimensionless with magnitude below 1; output frequency shares the input unit (Hz). This applies at the instant of closest approach where motion is exactly transverse; any radial component adds a classical Doppler shift.

name: Relativistic Doppler Effect (General Angle)
description: Computes the observed frequency for a source moving at beta and viewed at angle theta, combining the classical Doppler shift with relativistic time dilation. It reduces to the transverse effect at theta = pi/2 and the longitudinal effect along the line of motion.
notes: Theta is the observation angle in radians in the observer frame and beta is dimensionless below 1. Sign conventions for theta and beta determine whether the result is a blueshift or redshift, so check the geometry carefully.

name: Invariant Mass from Four-Momentum
description: Computes the invariant (rest) mass of a system from its total energy and momentum, as sqrt(Etot^2/c^4 - p^2/c^2). This Lorentz-invariant combination is the same in every reference frame.
notes: Energy in joules, momentum in kg*m/s, c in m/s give mass in kilograms. The quantity under the root must be non-negative; a negative value indicates inconsistent inputs rather than a physical mass.

name: Relativistic Momentum from Energy
description: Computes the relativistic momentum of a particle from its total energy and rest mass, as sqrt(Etot^2 - (m*c^2)^2) divided by c. It inverts the energy-momentum relation to recover momentum from the energy.
notes: Energy in joules, mass in kilograms, c in m/s give momentum in kg*m/s. Total energy must be at least the rest energy m*c^2, otherwise the square root has no real value.

name: Relativistic Energy (Momentum Form)
description: Computes the total relativistic energy of a particle from its momentum and rest mass, as sqrt((p*c)^2 + (m*c^2)^2). This is the energy-momentum relation combining kinetic and rest energy.
notes: Momentum in kg*m/s, mass in kilograms, c in m/s give energy in joules. For a massless particle it reduces to E = p*c; for zero momentum it gives the rest energy m*c^2.

name: Relativistic Doppler Shift (Wavelength, Receding)
description: Computes the observed wavelength from a source receding along the line of sight, as the rest wavelength times sqrt((1+beta)/(1-beta)). Recession stretches the wavelength, producing a redshift.
notes: Beta is dimensionless with magnitude below 1; output wavelength shares the input unit. This is the longitudinal (radial) receding form; motion at an angle requires the general-angle Doppler formula instead.

name: Relativistic Doppler Shift (Wavelength, Approaching)
description: Computes the observed wavelength from a source approaching along the line of sight, as the rest wavelength times sqrt((1-beta)/(1+beta)). Approach compresses the wavelength, producing a blueshift.
notes: Beta is dimensionless with magnitude below 1; output wavelength shares the input unit. This is the longitudinal approaching form; it is the reciprocal of the receding case for the same beta.

name: Gravitational Redshift (Schwarzschild)
description: Computes the gravitational redshift of light escaping from radius r around a mass M in the Schwarzschild metric, as 1/sqrt(1 - 2GM/(rc^2)) minus 1. It gives the fractional increase in wavelength seen far from the mass.
notes: Radius r must exceed the Schwarzschild radius 2GM/c^2 or the expression is imaginary. The result is the dimensionless redshift z; it diverges as r approaches the event horizon.

name: Schwarzschild Time Dilation Factor
description: Computes the gravitational time dilation factor at radius r around a mass M, as sqrt(1 - 2GM/(rc^2)). It is the ratio of proper time at r to coordinate time far away; clocks deeper in the gravity well run slower.
notes: Radius r must exceed the Schwarzschild radius 2GM/c^2 or the root is imaginary. The dimensionless factor approaches 1 far from the mass and drops to 0 at the event horizon.

name: Escape Velocity (Schwarzschild)
description: Computes the escape velocity from a spherical mass M at radius r, as sqrt(2GM/r), the speed needed to break free of its gravity. When this equals the speed of light, r is the Schwarzschild radius.
notes: SI units (G in N*m^2/kg^2, M in kg, r in m) give the result in m/s. This is the classical Newtonian escape speed; it coincidentally matches the Schwarzschild horizon condition but is not a relativistic derivation.

name: Photon Sphere Radius
description: Computes the radius of the photon sphere around a non-rotating black hole of mass M, as 3GM/c^2. At this radius light can orbit in an unstable circular path, equal to 1.5 times the Schwarzschild radius.
notes: SI units (G, M in kg, c in m/s) give the radius in meters. Valid for a Schwarzschild (non-rotating, uncharged) black hole; rotating Kerr black holes have direction-dependent photon orbits.

name: ISCO Radius (Schwarzschild)
description: Computes the radius of the innermost stable circular orbit around a Schwarzschild black hole of mass M, as 6GM/c^2. Inside this radius no stable circular orbit exists, so orbiting matter spirals inward.
notes: SI units (G, M in kg, c in m/s) give the radius in meters, equal to three Schwarzschild radii. Valid for a non-rotating black hole; spin shifts the ISCO inward for prograde and outward for retrograde orbits.

name: Gravitational Deflection of Light
description: Computes the general-relativistic deflection angle of a light ray grazing a mass M at impact parameter b, as 4GM/(bc^2). This is twice the Newtonian prediction and was confirmed by starlight bending near the Sun.
notes: SI units give the deflection in radians and it assumes a small angle with b well outside the Schwarzschild radius. The impact parameter b is the perpendicular distance of the undeflected ray from the mass center.

name: Shapiro Time Delay
description: Computes the extra light-travel time a signal accumulates when it passes close to a massive body, whose gravity warps spacetime. The delay grows with the deflector mass M and shrinks for larger impact parameter b, giving seconds of added round-trip time in the weak field.
notes: A weak-field, logarithmic approximation valid when the impact parameter b is much larger than the Schwarzschild radius. Distances d1 and d2 are measured from the deflector to source and observer along the line of sight.

name: Relativistic Perihelion Precession
description: Gives the general-relativistic advance of an orbit's perihelion per revolution, in radians. The precession increases with central mass M and orbital eccentricity, and decreases with the semi-major axis a, explaining Mercury's anomalous 43 arcsec-per-century drift.
notes: Result is radians accumulated each orbit; multiply by the number of orbits per century to compare with observed rates. Valid in the weak field for a nearly Keplerian orbit.

name: Chirp Mass (Gravitational Waves)
description: Combines the two component masses of an inspiraling binary into the single chirp mass that controls how fast its gravitational-wave frequency sweeps upward. It weights the product and sum of m1 and m2 so that this one number governs the observed waveform.
notes: Inputs and result share the same mass unit (kg here); the value is symmetric in m1 and m2. It sets the leading-order inspiral rate but does not by itself give the individual masses.

name: Gravitational Wave Luminosity (Quadrupole)
description: Estimates the power radiated as gravitational waves by two point masses in a circular orbit, using the quadrupole formula. The output in watts rises steeply with the masses and falls as the fifth power of their separation r, so it dominates only in tight, massive binaries.
notes: Assumes a Newtonian circular orbit and point masses; it is an order-of-magnitude approximation that breaks down near merger. Extremely sensitive to r through the 1/r^5 factor.

name: Schwarzschild Surface Gravity
description: Gives the surface gravity of a non-rotating black hole at its event horizon as c^4/(4GM). The value in m/s squared is inversely proportional to mass, so larger black holes have weaker horizon gravity.
notes: This is the standard surface gravity kappa (as an acceleration), not the tidal force felt by an infalling observer. It applies to the Schwarzschild horizon only, with no spin or charge.

name: Hawking Temperature
description: Computes the temperature of the thermal radiation a Schwarzschild black hole emits from quantum effects at its horizon. The temperature in kelvin is inversely proportional to mass M, so a solar-mass black hole is fantastically cold, far below the CMB.
notes: Applies to a non-rotating, uncharged black hole. Larger black holes are colder; the tiny values make astrophysical black holes effectively non-evaporating today.

name: Black Hole Evaporation Time
description: Estimates how long a Schwarzschild black hole takes to fully evaporate via Hawking radiation, in seconds. The lifetime scales as the cube of the mass M, so heavier black holes last vastly longer while tiny ones vanish quickly.
notes: Assumes only Hawking emission with no infalling matter and ignores CMB heating, which would prevent evaporation of stellar-mass holes today. Strongly sensitive to M through the M^3 factor.

name: Kretschmann Scalar (Schwarzschild)
description: Gives the Kretschmann curvature scalar of the Schwarzschild geometry, a coordinate-independent measure of spacetime curvature. In units of 1/m^4 it grows as 1/r^6, diverging at the central singularity and staying finite and smooth at the horizon.
notes: The finite value at the event horizon shows the horizon is a coordinate artifact, not a true singularity; only r=0 is a genuine curvature singularity. Radius r is the areal radial coordinate.

name: Relativistic Larmor Power
description: Computes the power radiated by an accelerating charge at relativistic speeds for acceleration parallel to velocity, in watts. It generalizes the Larmor formula with a gamma^6 factor, so radiation grows enormously as the Lorentz factor increases.
notes: The gamma^6 scaling holds for linear (parallel) acceleration; perpendicular acceleration carries a gamma^4 factor instead. Here a is the proper acceleration and q the particle charge.

name: Thomas Precession Rate
description: Gives the rate at which a moving particle's spin axis precesses purely from special-relativistic velocity composition, in radians per second. It depends on the Lorentz factor and on acceleration perpendicular to velocity, and vanishes when the two are parallel.
notes: This is the magnitude for acceleration perpendicular to velocity; a and v should be the perpendicular components. It is a kinematic effect distinct from any torque on the spin.

name: Relativistic Cyclotron Frequency
description: Computes the angular gyration frequency of a charged particle in a magnetic field once its relativistic mass increase is included, as qB/(gamma m). The frequency in rad/s drops as the Lorentz factor gamma rises, so fast particles orbit more slowly.
notes: Divide by 2*pi to get the frequency in Hz. The gamma factor reduces the non-relativistic cyclotron frequency; m is the rest mass and B the field magnitude.

name: Bondi k-Factor
description: Computes the relativistic Doppler k-factor sqrt((1+beta)/(1-beta)), the ratio by which signal intervals stretch or compress between observers in relative motion. Values above one indicate recession (redshift) and below one indicate approach.
notes: The input beta is the speed as a fraction of c and must satisfy -1 < beta < 1. This longitudinal factor equals the relativistic Doppler shift ratio in Bondi's k-calculus.

name: Gravitational Redshift (Weak Field)
description: Computes the fractional shift in a photon's frequency as it climbs a height h in a weak, uniform gravitational field, as gh/c^2. The dimensionless result gives how much light is redshifted going up (or blueshifted going down).
notes: A weak-field approximation valid when gh is much smaller than c^2. The result is the fractional shift delta_f/f, not a frequency; multiply by the base frequency to get the actual shift.

name: Sagnac Effect Time Difference
description: Gives the arrival-time difference between two light beams traveling in opposite directions around a rotating loop, as 4*A*omega/c^2. The result in seconds is proportional to the enclosed area A and the angular velocity, and underlies ring-laser and fiber-optic gyroscopes.
notes: A is the area enclosed by the loop and omega its rotation rate; the effect is independent of the loop shape. The default omega matches Earth's rotation. The value is a tiny time difference.

name: Relativistic Momentum (Rapidity Form)
description: Computes a particle's relativistic momentum expressed through rapidity, as m*c*sinh(phi). Because the hyperbolic sine of rapidity equals gamma*beta, this reproduces the usual momentum while adding rapidities linearly instead of velocities.
notes: The bracket (exp(phi) - exp(-phi))/2 is sinh(phi); rapidity phi is dimensionless and additive under boosts. Result is in kg*m/s for mass in kg.

name: Relativistic Energy (Rapidity Form)
description: Gives a particle's total relativistic energy in terms of rapidity, as m*c^2*cosh(phi). Since the hyperbolic cosine of rapidity equals the Lorentz factor gamma, this equals gamma*m*c^2 and reduces to the rest energy when the rapidity is zero.
notes: The bracket (exp(phi) + exp(-phi))/2 is cosh(phi), which equals gamma. Result is in joules for mass in kg; at phi=0 it returns the rest energy m*c^2.

name: Unruh Temperature
description: Computes the temperature of the thermal bath a uniformly accelerating observer perceives in vacuum, as hbar*a/(2*pi*c*kB). The temperature in kelvin is proportional to the proper acceleration a, linking acceleration to an apparent thermal glow.
notes: Input a is the proper acceleration; even 1e20 m/s^2 gives only a fraction of a kelvin, so the effect is minuscule at everyday accelerations. It is the accelerated-frame analog of Hawking temperature.

name: Gravitational Wave Strain (Order Estimate)
description: Provides an order-of-magnitude estimate of the gravitational-wave strain at distance r from a source, as 4*G*Ekin/(c^4*r). The dimensionless strain scales with the non-spherical kinetic energy Ekin and falls off as 1/r.
notes: A rough scaling estimate, not a precise waveform; only the non-spherically-symmetric part of the kinetic energy radiates. Result is the fractional length change h, typically around 1e-21 at Earth.

name: Geodetic Precession Rate
description: Gives the geodetic (de Sitter) precession rate of a gyroscope orbiting a mass, as 3*G*M*v/(2*c^2*r^2). This general-relativistic effect in rad/s arises from parallel transport of the spin through curved spacetime and was confirmed by Gravity Probe B.
notes: A weak-field expression; here v is the orbital velocity and r the orbital radius. It is distinct from frame-dragging (Lense-Thirring), which depends on the central body's spin.

name: Lense-Thirring Precession
description: Computes the frame-dragging precession rate caused by a rotating mass's angular momentum J, as 2*G*J/(c^2*r^3). The result in rad/s shows how a spinning body twists nearby spacetime, precessing gyroscopes and orbits.
notes: A weak-field expression that falls off as 1/r^3; J is the central body's angular momentum. This is distinct from geodetic precession, which arises from the body's mass rather than its spin.

name: Kerr Outer Horizon Radius
description: Gives the outer event-horizon radius of a rotating (Kerr) black hole, as G*M*(1 + sqrt(1 - astar^2))/c^2. Increasing the dimensionless spin astar shrinks the horizon from the Schwarzschild value toward half of it at maximal spin.
notes: The dimensionless spin astar must satisfy |astar| <= 1, or the square root becomes imaginary and no horizon exists (a naked singularity). At astar=0 it returns the Schwarzschild radius.

name: Relativistic Rocket Velocity
