description: Computes the velocity of a rocket undergoing constant proper acceleration a, as c*tanh(a*t/c) in coordinate time t. The speed rises linearly at first but saturates just below the speed of light no matter how long the burn continues.
notes: The expression equals c*tanh(a*t/c); t is coordinate (Earth-frame) time, not the traveler's proper time. Result stays strictly below c. Default a is one Earth gravity.

name: Relativistic Rocket Distance
description: Gives the distance covered by a rocket under constant proper acceleration a, as (c^2/a)*(cosh(a*t/c) - 1) in coordinate time t. For long times the distance grows almost linearly (near light speed) after an early quadratic phase.
notes: The bracket equals cosh(a*t/c) - 1; t is coordinate time measured in the launch frame. Distance is in meters for SI inputs. Default a is one Earth gravity.

name: Relativistic Rocket Proper Time
description: Computes the proper time experienced aboard a rocket with constant proper acceleration a after a given coordinate time t, as (c/a)*arcsinh(a*t/c). It grows only logarithmically for large t, so the crew ages far less than mission clocks on Earth.
notes: The logarithm term equals arcsinh(a*t/c); t is the coordinate (Earth-frame) time and the result is the shipboard elapsed time. Default a is one Earth gravity.

name: Center-of-Mass Energy (Fixed Target)
description: Estimates the center-of-mass collision energy in a fixed-target experiment, as sqrt(2*m*c^2*Eb) for beam energy Eb striking a stationary mass m. It grows only as the square root of beam energy, which is why colliders outperform fixed targets.
notes: A high-energy approximation valid when the beam energy Eb greatly exceeds the target rest energy m*c^2. Eb is the beam's total energy; result is in joules for SI inputs.

name: Relativistic Speed from Kinetic Energy
description: Recovers a particle's speed as a fraction of c from its kinetic energy, as sqrt(1 - 1/(1 + KE/(m*c^2))^2). The result beta approaches 1 as the kinetic energy grows far beyond the rest energy m*c^2.
notes: Result is the dimensionless ratio beta = v/c, not a velocity; multiply by c for m/s. KE is kinetic energy and m the rest mass. Valid for any positive KE.

name: Lorentz Factor from Kinetic Energy
description: Gives the Lorentz factor gamma of a particle directly from its kinetic energy, as 1 + KE/(m*c^2). Since total energy is gamma*m*c^2 and kinetic energy is the excess over rest energy, the ratio KE/(m*c^2) simply adds to one.
notes: The dimensionless result is at least 1; it equals 1 when KE is zero (particle at rest). KE is kinetic energy and m the rest mass, in consistent SI units.

name: GPS Relativistic Frequency Shift
description: Estimates the fractional frequency difference between a GPS satellite clock and one on Earth's surface, combining gravitational blueshift with the satellite's time-dilation term. The gravitational part speeds the orbiting clock while its motion slows it, netting a small positive shift.
notes: A weak-field approximation; the result is a dimensionless fractional rate that must be corrected for GPS to work. Uses potential difference between surface radius rE and orbit radius rsat plus the velocity term.

name: Radiation Inverse-Square Law
description: Gives radiation intensity at a new distance from a point source using the inverse-square law: reference intensity times the square of the ratio of reference distance to actual distance. Doubling the distance quarters the intensity.
notes: Applies to an ideal point source in a non-attenuating medium; it ignores absorption and scattering. Distances d and d0 must share the same unit, and d must be non-zero.

name: Radiation Shielding Attenuation
description: Computes the transmitted radiation intensity through a shield using exponential attenuation: incident intensity times e raised to the power of negative attenuation coefficient times thickness. Thicker or denser shields transmit exponentially less.
notes: The linear attenuation coefficient mu and thickness x must use reciprocal length units (e.g. 1/cm and cm). Valid for narrow-beam geometry; it omits buildup from scattered radiation, so real shielding may transmit more.

name: Particle in a 3-D Box Energy
expression: h_planck^2 / (8 * m * l^2) * (nx^2 + ny^2 + nz^2) / q_e
description: Gives the energy level of a particle in a cubic box with infinitely high walls; different (n_x, n_y, n_z) with the same sum of squares are degenerate.
notes: An electron in a 1 nm box has a ground state of about 1.13 eV.

name: Quantum Dot Band Gap (Brus Equation)
description: Estimates the band gap of a spherical semiconductor nanocrystal: bulk gap + confinement − electron–hole attraction (Brus 1984).
notes: Smaller dots emit bluer light — the principle of QLED displays.

name: Landau Level Energy
description: Gives the energy of a Landau level, ħω_c(n + ½), for a charged particle confined to a plane in a magnetic field.
notes: The spacing in GaAs at 10 T is about 17 meV — the stage for the quantum Hall effect.

name: Josephson Frequency
description: Gives the frequency of the alternating supercurrent through a Josephson junction held at a DC voltage: 483.6 MHz per µV.
notes: The basis of the international voltage standard.

name: Quantum Hall Resistance
description: Gives the quantised Hall resistance on a plateau: the von Klitzing constant 25,812.807 Ω divided by the filling factor.
notes: Defines the ohm in the SI since 2019.

name: Positronium Energy Level
description: Gives the energy levels of positronium (an electron bound to a positron): half those of hydrogen because the reduced mass is mₑ/2.
notes: Ground state −6.80 eV.

name: Klein–Nishina Differential Cross Section
description: Gives the probability per solid angle that a photon Compton-scatters off a free electron at angle θ (Klein and Nishina 1929).
notes: At low energy it becomes the Thomson result; at high energy scattering is mostly forward.

name: BCS Superconducting Energy Gap
description: Gives the zero-temperature energy gap Δ(0) ≈ 1.764 k_B T_c of a conventional superconductor from BCS theory (1957).
notes: Niobium (9.25 K) gives about 1.41 meV.

name: Intrinsic Carrier Concentration
expression: sqrt(nc * nv) * exp(-eg * q_e / (2 * k_boltz * t))
description: Gives the electron (and hole) density in a pure semiconductor: about 10¹⁰ per cm³ for silicon at room temperature.
notes: Rises steeply with temperature — why chips leak more when hot.

name: Drude Electrical Conductivity
description: Gives a metal's conductivity from the free-electron (Drude 1900) model: σ = ne²τ/m.
notes: Copper: about 6 × 10⁷ S/m.

name: Carrier Mobility from Relaxation Time
description: Gives the drift mobility μ = eτ/m* of electrons or holes in a semiconductor.
notes: Silicon electrons are about 1400 cm²/(V·s) at room temperature.

name: Semiconductor Conductivity
description: Gives the conductivity of a doped semiconductor from its carrier densities and mobilities.
notes: Doping 1 in 5 million silicon atoms raises the conductivity about a million-fold.

name: Solar Cell Open-Circuit Voltage
expression: nf * k_boltz * t / q_e * ln(il / is0 + 1)
description: Gives the voltage of a solar cell with no load from its light current and dark saturation current.
notes: Falls about 2 mV per °C for silicon — hot panels produce less.

name: Shockley–Queisser-Style Photon Energy Limit: Cut-off Wavelength
description: Gives the longest wavelength a semiconductor with band gap E_g can absorb; longer (redder) light passes through.
notes: Silicon (1.12 eV) stops absorbing beyond about 1107 nm.

name: Alpha Particle Range in Air (Geiger Rule)
description: Gives the approximate range of an alpha particle in air at normal conditions, valid for about 4–7 MeV.
notes: A sheet of paper or a few cm of air stop alphas.

name: Distance of Closest Approach (Head-On Collision)
description: Gives how close a charged particle fired straight at a nucleus gets before being turned back — Rutherford's upper bound on nuclear size.
notes: A 5 MeV alpha stops about 45 fm from a gold nucleus.

name: D–T Fusion Energy from Fuel Mass
description: Gives the energy released by fusing a mass of equal-molar deuterium–tritium fuel, 17.59 MeV per reaction.
notes: One gram releases about 3.4 × 10¹¹ J — as much as about 8 tonnes of oil.

name: Fusion Triple Product Ratio to Ignition
description: Compares a plasma's density × temperature × confinement time with the D–T ignition value of about 3 × 10²¹ keV·s/m³ (Lawson criterion).
notes: 1 or more means the plasma could sustain itself.

name: Potassium–Argon Age
description: Dates volcanic rock from the ratio of argon-40 to potassium-40, using the half-life 1.248 billion years and the 10.9 % branch to argon.
notes: Works for rocks older than about 100,000 years.

name: Uranium–Lead Age (²⁰⁶Pb/²³⁸U)
description: Dates a mineral such as zircon from its lead-206 to uranium-238 ratio (decay constant 1.55125 × 10⁻¹⁰ per year).
notes: A ratio of 1 means one half-life: about 4.47 billion years.

name: Twin Paradox Age Difference
description: Gives how much younger a traveller is than a stay-at-home twin after a round trip at constant speed (ignoring acceleration phases).
notes: A 4-light-year trip at 0.87c saves the traveller about 4.6 years.

name: Muon Survival with Time Dilation
description: Gives the fraction of muons surviving a flight through the atmosphere, using their dilated lifetime γτ (τ = 2.197 µs).
notes: Without time dilation almost none would reach the ground — the classic evidence for special relativity.

name: Relativistic Beaming Half-Angle
description: Gives the half-angle 1/γ of the forward cone into which a fast-moving source concentrates half its radiation.
notes: Why jets pointing at us look far brighter than those pointing away.

name: Average Logarithmic Energy Loss per Collision (ξ)

variables.label: Mass number of the moderator nucleus

description: Gives the average decrease in the logarithm of neutron energy per elastic collision with a nucleus of mass number A.
notes: Hydrogen (A = 1) gives ξ = 1; carbon about 0.158.

name: Collisions to Thermalise a Neutron
description: Gives the average number of collisions to slow a fission neutron to thermal energy in a moderator.
notes: About 18 in water (hydrogen), 115 in graphite.

name: Plasma Beta
description: Gives the ratio of plasma pressure to magnetic pressure — how efficiently a magnetic field confines a plasma.
notes: Tokamaks run at a few percent.
